action_criteria.rationale: Embolic-pattern infarcts with a sinus-rhythm ECG and frequent atrial ectopy: about 30 days of monitoring is reasonable and finding AF changes treatment to anticoagulation.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not accept a single sinus-rhythm ECG as excluding atrial fibrillation in a patient with infarcts in more than one territory
Do not continue aspirin together with the anticoagulant without a separate coronary indication
Do not withhold anticoagulation because the atrial fibrillation is paroxysmal or its burden is low [ESC_AF_2024]
Do not treat this as small-vessel disease on the strength of Fazekas 1 change
Do not leave a driving decision to the patient's own restriction when a visuospatial deficit is documented
required_recommendations: Start a DOAC for the paroxysmal atrial fibrillation (CHA2DS2-VA 4: age 73, hypertension, prior stroke), e.g. apixaban 5 mg twice daily (no dose-reduction criterion: age under 80, weight 70 kg, creatinine 0.86 mg/dL), and stop aspirin [AHA_ASA_2021_secondary]
Lower blood pressure (150/86 mmHg) gradually to below 130/80 mmHg, checking orthostatic BP at each change [AHA_ASA_2021_secondary]

Intensify lipid lowering from atorvastatin 20 mg to a high-intensity statin, aiming at LDL below 55 mg/dL (current 116 mg/dL): very high risk after ischaemic strokes at 73 with hypertension and carotid plaque; add ezetimibe if the goal is not reached [ACC_AHA_dyslipidemia_2026]
Reattribute the visual episode previously called migraine to cerebral ischaemia in the left posterior cerebral territory, which makes the infarcts bihemispheric
Arrange formal visual field testing and a formal driving assessment before she drives again, given the occipital infarct and the visuoconstructional deficit

avoided_actions.rationale: No rapidly progressive or fluctuating course and no episode suggesting seizures; EEG has no diagnostic role in this stepwise decline.
No parkinsonism, fluctuations, hallucinations or dream enactment; a dopamine transporter scan does not address the vascular question.
No feature of Lewy body disease or autonomic failure; cardiac sympathetic imaging does not inform this diagnosis.
A chronic stepwise decline dated to two focal events, not a subacute multidomain syndrome: an untargeted paraneoplastic or autoimmune battery has no indication.
MRI is available and not contraindicated; CT cannot show microbleeds, siderosis or small lacunes.

accepted: Vascular dementia: multi-infarct type, cardioembolic, secondary to paroxysmal atrial fibrillation identified on prolonged monitoring
major neurocognitive disorder due to vascular disease

differential.key_features: Stepwise course with dateable events, cue-responsive recall, preserved medial temporal lobes, and three infarcts that account for the deficits
Fazekas 1 burden is far below the threshold for attributing a dementia to small-vessel disease
No haemodynamically significant carotid disease, and no single artery can supply two territories in opposite hemispheres
The visual episode was attributed to migraine in a patient with no migraine history; the left occipital infarct on MRI is the explanation
No fluctuation, hallucinations, parkinsonism or dream enactment

key_clinical_evidence: One ECG in sinus rhythm excludes nothing: paroxysmal atrial fibrillation is by definition intermittent, and in an unexplained multi-territory infarct pattern the yield of prolonged monitoring justifies it
Frequent premature atrial complexes are a marker of atrial cardiopathy and raise the pre-test probability of paroxysmal fibrillation
The lesion distribution — two territories, opposite hemispheres — is what makes the search for a proximal source obligatory
Checking SWI for microbleeds is part of the anticoagulation decision, not an academic exercise
A visual episode labelled migraine in a patient who has never had migraine deserves re-examination; here the occipital infarct explains it and adds a second territory to the count

red_herrings.data_point: A single ECG in sinus rhythm

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: She has no migraine history, and the left occipital infarct on MRI places the episode in the left posterior cerebral territory, adding a second arterial territory
red_herrings.data_point: A previous diagnosis of migraine with aura
red_herrings.intended_effect: Removes the visual episode from the vascular count and keeps the infarct burden apparently confined to one hemisphere

sequence_constraints.reason: Document the cognitive deficit before attributing it: imaging read without a cognitive profile invites over-attribution of incidental white matter change.

patient.history_present_illness: Mrs. Chiara Venturi is a 73-year-old retired French teacher who attends with her husband. Three years ago she was admitted elsewhere with left arm weakness and inattention to the left side; she was told she had had a stroke, was discharged on aspirin, and no cardiac monitoring beyond an inpatient ECG was performed. Her husband dates the first change to the months after that admission: she stopped preparing lessons for the private pupils she still taught, and began to need lists for tasks she had always held in her head. Fourteen months ago she had twenty minutes of blurred vision in the right field, which was attributed to migraine although she has never had migraine. In the weeks after it she gave up the private teaching altogether and twice mislaid the household bills. Between the two events she was stable, and her husband is emphatic that the changes were sudden rather than gradual. Her memory improves with prompting about context; her difficulty is with planning and with holding several things in mind. She has no headache, no seizures, no hallucinations, no fluctuation in alertness and no dream enactment. Her pulse is regular today at 76, though frequent extra beats are palpable, and she has never been told she has an irregular heartbeat.
